The powertrain control module (PCM) has fuel-pump command and monitor connections. Fused feeds and the relay in the battery junction box provide the energy path, separate from the information used to control operation.

sections.title: Pressure and fuel level answer different questions
sections.body: The fuel tank pressure (FTP) sensor has reference, return, and signal connections to report tank pressure conditions. The fuel sender instead supplies level information to the instrument panel cluster (IPC). Keeping these functions separate prevents a tank-pressure circuit from being confused with either fuel quantity or pressure at the engine’s injectors.

sections.title: Reading the control and supply branches
sections.body: The body control module (BCM) appears with field-effect transistor (FET) fuel-pump control outputs. Ground, shield, splice, and continuation markings show how the circuits relate beyond this page. Always-live labels apply to the indicated feeds; they do not mean the pump itself should run continuously whenever the battery is connected.

topics.title: 3.7L Camshaft and Knock Sensor Wiring
topics.summary: This 3.7L engine-control sheet connects camshaft-position and knock-sensing circuits to the Powertrain Control Module (PCM). These inputs describe engine timing and vibration conditions used in electronic engine management.

sections.title: Position and vibration tell different stories
sections.body: Camshaft Position (CMP) sensors report the rotational position of the camshafts, allowing the controller to relate valve timing to engine operation. Knock Sensor (KS) circuits report vibration information used to recognize combustion knock. The sheet separates the camshaft inputs by bank and sensor designation.

sections.title: Sensor connections are not all alike
sections.body: The drawing shows differing connection arrangements among the camshaft sensors, along with paired knock-sensor paths. It also identifies supply and return circuits. Those distinctions matter because a powered sensor connection and a paired sensing circuit cannot be understood simply by assuming every sensor has the same wiring.

sections.title: Follow bank and sensor labels
sections.body: The bank and sensor designations identify which input reaches each PCM connection; they do not themselves establish physical left-and-right locations. Shared circuit identifiers, splices and continuations show relationships extending beyond this sheet. The schematic traces electrical connections, while a component-location reference is needed to find the corresponding hardware.

topics.title: Timing, purge and temperature circuits on the 3.7L
topics.summary: This 3.7L engine-control sheet brings together camshaft-timing solenoids, the fuel-vapor purge valve and the cylinder-head temperature sensor. It shows how their separate functions connect to shared power distribution and engine management.

sections.title: The components perform different engine jobs
sections.body: Variable Camshaft Timing (VCT) solenoids control oil flow used to change valve timing. The evaporative emissions (EVAP) purge valve meters stored fuel vapor toward the intake. The Cylinder Head Temperature (CHT) sensor reports thermal conditions. Their signals and commands help engine management coordinate valve operation, vapor consumption and temperature-dependent decisions.

sections.title: Shared power connects otherwise distinct functions
sections.body: The Battery Junction Box (BJB) supplies a protected feed that branches toward several controlled components. The Powertrain Control Module (PCM) has separate connections for the individual timing solenoids, purge valve and temperature information. A shared feed can affect several loads, while an individual control or sensor path has a narrower electrical role.

sections.title: Follow bank and transmission qualifications
sections.body: The timing-solenoid names distinguish both engine banks and their individual solenoids. Manual- and automatic-transmission labels qualify branches and continuations, so those paths should remain associated with the correct configuration. Hot in start or run describes feed availability; connector and continuation references connect this sheet to the rest of the 3.7L circuit.

topics.title: Oxygen Sensor and Transmission Temperature Wiring
topics.summary: This engine-control sheet connects heated oxygen sensors and a transmission-temperature sensor to the powertrain control module (PCM). It separates sensing circuits from heater circuits so their different electrical jobs can be understood.

sections.title: Measurement and heating use different paths
sections.body: A heated oxygen sensor (HO2S) measures oxygen-related conditions in the exhaust, while its heater helps bring the sensing element to operating temperature. The transmission fluid temperature (TFT) input instead describes transmission heat. These are different measurements even though their circuits appear together at the same controller.

sections.title: A sensor housing can contain separate circuits
sections.body: Each oxygen-sensor connection includes both sensing and heater functions. The heater supply is marked as powered during starting or running, while signal return (SIGRTN) provides the reference path for measurement. Distinguishing those roles prevents a heater-circuit concern from being mistaken for direct evidence about exhaust oxygen content.

sections.title: Respect the transmission qualification
sections.body: The temperature-sensor branch is labeled for a manual transmission. Oxygen-sensor identifiers distinguish the two assemblies, and heater labels identify their corresponding control paths. Continuation marks show connections to other engine-control sheets. These labels define electrical applicability and identity without showing the sensors' actual mounting positions.

topics.title: Cruise-control signals through the steering wheel
topics.summary: The steering-wheel cruise switches let the driver request a maintained road speed and change cruise-control modes. This sheet shows how those requests reach the steering-column electronics on vehicles without adaptive cruise control.

sections.title: Buttons request a change in speed control
sections.body: The left lower switch group contains the on, off, set, cancel and resume controls. The Steering Column Control Module (SCCM) receives these inputs and passes cruise requests onward to the Powertrain Control Module (PCM). The PCM controls engine output to maintain the requested speed within the system's operating limits.

sections.title: The clockspring bridges the rotating wheel
sections.body: The clockspring maintains electrical connections while the steering wheel turns. Its flexible internal connection allows switch signals to cross from the rotating wheel to the fixed column wiring. Showing that junction makes the sheet useful for understanding the complete input path rather than treating the button and column module as directly adjacent connections.

sections.title: Distinguish inputs, returns and illumination
sections.body: The analog-to-digital (A/D) channel labels identify inputs interpreted by the column module, and RETURN identifies their associated return path. Audio, navigation and illumination references lead to related sheets for other steering-wheel functions. The WITHOUT ADAPTIVE CRUISE label limits applicability; this drawing does not describe adaptive distance-control operation.

topics.title: Door and B-pillar side-impact sensor circuits
topics.summary: Side-impact sensors provide crash information to the restraints control module (RCM). This sheet identifies separate driver-door and passenger-door sensor circuits, plus left-hand and right-hand B-pillar sensor circuits within a coupe-only branch.

sections.title: Sensors inform the restraint decision
sections.body: The supplemental restraint system (SRS) uses sensor information to assess a crash and determine whether appropriate restraints should deploy. A side-impact sensor supplies an input to that decision; it is not itself an airbag. Separate sensor identities allow the controller to distinguish information arriving from different parts of the vehicle.

sections.title: Dedicated feed and return pairs matter
sections.body: The sheet labels a feed and return for each sensor connection at the RCM. Door-sensor circuits also pass through identified inline connections. Those distinctions help locate the electrical path named in a diagnostic reference without confusing the driver-side, passenger-side, door or pillar sensor with another component.

sections.title: Use the schematic within the restraint procedure
sections.body: The dashed coupe outline surrounds only the B-pillar sensor circuits; the door-sensor circuits appear outside that outline. Keep this qualification with those B-pillar branches rather than applying it to the entire sheet. Connector references support identification, not an invitation to test them independently. The page requires consultation of the workshop manual because improper restraint-circuit troubleshooting can cause unintended deployment and injury.

topics.title: Driver Seat and Belt Restraint Inputs
topics.summary: This Supplemental Restraint System (SRS) sheet shows the driver seat-position sensor and safety-belt buckle switch connections. Their signals inform the Restraints Control Module (RCM) about seat position and buckle status as part of its wider restraint monitoring.

sections.title: Knowing how the driver is positioned
sections.body: The seat-position sensor reports information about the seat’s position along its track, while the buckle switch reports whether the belt is latched. These are different observations about the occupant’s situation. The RCM combines sensor information across the restraint system when monitoring operation and determining the appropriate response to a crash.

sections.title: Why the inputs share a diagram
sections.body: Both components are associated with the driver’s seat area, but each has a distinct signal role at the RCM. The sheet identifies the driver track-position and buckle-switch paths along with their return connections. A return provides an electrical reference; it does not make the connected sensors the same circuit or component.

sections.title: Using the schematic within restraint procedures
sections.body: Connector and splice identifiers help match the seat-area wiring to the controller connections. The sheet’s warning makes the workshop-manual diagnostic sequence essential because incorrect restraint-circuit work can cause unintended deployment. This drawing is an identification and tracing aid, not a stand-alone instruction to probe, disconnect or energize the pictured circuits.

topics.title: Manual Climate Control Interface Wiring
topics.summary: This sheet shows electrical connections around the Front Controls Interface Module (FCIM) in the manual climate-control system. It also identifies nearby starting, hazard, rear-window heating and illumination circuits that share this control area.

sections.title: Cabin sensing and driver controls
sections.body: The in-vehicle temperature sensor provides information about cabin conditions, and the sheet also names humidity and motor-related connections. The FCIM brings these paths together with driver controls. Separate labels distinguish sensing information from functions such as the rear-defrost request, so similar-looking wires do not imply interchangeable jobs.

sections.title: Why other systems appear here
sections.body: The same interface area includes start-button channels, hazard controls and backlighting, which explains the references to starting, hazard lamps and panel illumination. Their presence does not make them climate actuators. This sheet helps identify where a circuit leaves the interface and continues into the system responsible for that function.

sections.title: Reading supply and continuation labels
sections.body: The Body Control Module (BCM), fuse reference and 'Hot in Start or Run' label describe the shown supply relationship. Connector names and wire identifiers distinguish the individual paths. Lettered and numbered continuations lead to other sheets; they describe circuit continuity rather than physical wire routing behind the dashboard.

topics.title: Compressor control in the manual climate system
topics.summary: The air-conditioning (A/C) compressor circulates refrigerant so the system can remove heat from cabin air. This manual-climate sheet shows compressor-related electrical control, including clutch circuitry and an engine-specific compressor-control solenoid.

sections.title: Driver settings still involve engine electronics
sections.body: Manual climate controls let the driver select settings, but compressor operation still involves the Powertrain Control Module (PCM). The clutch field coil creates magnetic force to engage the compressor drive. The separately shown control solenoid regulates compressor operation on the applicable configuration, so clutch engagement and compressor regulation represent different electrical functions.

sections.title: The sheet joins control and power paths
sections.body: The Battery Junction Box (BJB) contains the clutch relay and protected supply shown here. Ground completes the load circuit, while the PCM has control connections and high-speed Controller Area Network (CAN) communication paths. These relationships explain how a climate request involves both engine coordination and electrical energy delivered to compressor components.

sections.title: Keep engine-specific paths separate
sections.body: The sheet includes 2.3L and 3.7L labels, with the compressor-control solenoid shown for the 2.3L arrangement. Those qualifications prevent one compressor configuration from being assumed for every engine. Hot at all times and hot in start or run identify supply conditions, while continuation references lead to the remaining control circuits.

topics.title: How sunlight informs automatic climate control
topics.summary: The sunload sensor detects sunlight that adds heat to the cabin. This diagram shows its driver-side and passenger-side connections to the automatic climate controls, together with its automatic-lighting connections.

sections.title: Sunlight adds heat unevenly
sections.body: Sunlight can warm your face, clothing and interior surfaces even when cabin air temperature has barely changed. Separate driver and passenger sunload signals give the Front Controls Interface Module (FCIM) information about that extra heating, allowing automatic climate control to account for sunlight reaching each side.

sections.title: One sensor serves related functions
sections.body: The sheet also connects the sensor's AUTOLAMP and RETURN paths to the Body Control Module (BCM). Automatic lighting responds to outside light conditions, while sunload information concerns cabin heating. Showing these paths together explains why a single sensor connection can be relevant to more than one system.

sections.title: Follow the named signal paths
sections.body: Read SUNLOAD DRV as the driver-side signal and SUNLOAD PASS as the passenger-side signal. Connector identifiers and wire colors distinguish those paths from the automatic-lighting and return circuits. The drawing describes electrical relationships; it does not show where sunlight reaches the sensor or how its harness runs through the car.

topics.title: Convertible rear-window and mirror heating circuits
topics.summary: The rear-window heater and heated mirrors use electrical resistance to warm their surfaces and improve visibility. This convertible wiring sheet shows the defrost relay, control connection, protected supplies and ground paths, with additional equipment qualifications on the mirror branches.

sections.title: Electrical resistance produces useful heat
sections.body: Current flowing through the rear-window element produces heat in the glass, helping clear condensation and frost. Mirror heating works on the same basic principle. Because heating requires appreciable electrical energy, the drawing includes protected supply paths and a relay rather than depicting the dashboard control as carrying every heater's operating current.

sections.title: The relay separates request from load
sections.body: The Front Controls Interface Module (FCIM) connects to the rear-window defrost relay circuit in the Battery Junction Box (BJB). The sheet also shows the mirror branches and their grounds. Displaying these paths together helps explain how a control request, a supply problem and a local heater connection represent different possible circuit concerns.

sections.title: Read the variant and supply labels carefully
sections.body: The CONVERTIBLE heading applies to this sheet. Within it, the dashed mirror-branch outlines identify the without-memory arrangement and the right-hand-drive alternative. Those local labels must stay with their respective branches. Hot at all times and hot in start or run describe different supply conditions. Connector and ground references connect the schematic to identification pages; the repeated mirror symbols show labeled alternatives rather than extra mirrors.

topics.title: Heated Exterior Mirror Circuits
topics.summary: This heated-window sheet covers the exterior mirror heating circuits for the memory-equipped arrangement shown. Electrical heating warms the mirror glass to help remove condensation or ice that obscures the rearward view.

sections.title: Heat comes from electrical resistance
sections.body: A heating element converts electrical current into heat behind the mirror surface. Each mirror needs a controlled feed and a complete return path for that current to flow. The sheet identifies separate driver and passenger heated-mirror outputs, allowing the two sides to be followed individually.

sections.title: The door modules supply each side
sections.body: The Driver Door Module (DDM) and Passenger Door Module (PDM) appear with their respective heated-mirror circuits. This explains why a mirror-heating concern can involve door-module wiring as well as the mirror itself. The page belongs to the heated-window section but specifically documents these exterior-mirror branches.

sections.title: Match the mirror, connector and return
sections.body: Left-hand and right-hand mirror labels keep the branches distinct, while connector, splice and ground identifiers show their electrical relationships. The memory qualifier defines the arrangement represented here. Cross-references provide further mirror information; the schematic alone does not establish heating activation conditions or the physical harness route.

topics.title: Headlamp switch and panel illumination
topics.summary: The headlamp switch combines exterior-lighting selections with panel-dimming controls and its own illumination. This diagram shows those distinct circuits connecting the switch, body control module (BCM), power supply, and grounds.

sections.title: A control with several electrical jobs
sections.body: The switch provides requests for lighting modes and brighter or dimmer panel lighting. Its backlighting also needs an electrical feed and return so the controls can be seen. The separate DIM, ILLUM, power, and ground labels distinguish a driver request from the electricity used to illuminate the switch.

sections.title: Why lighting requests appear together
sections.body: Headlamp on, headlamp off, parking lamps, automatic lamps, and fog-lamp requests share this switch assembly. Showing them beside illumination makes it possible to understand how one physical control participates in several circuits. A problem with one function does not establish that every part of the switch has failed.

sections.title: Separating options and continuations
sections.body: C205 identifies the headlamp-switch connector, and C2280B identifies the BCM connection shown. Ground references lead to G200 and G202, while the continuation leads to another illumination sheet. Rear fog lamps and headlamp leveling are equipment qualifiers; their presence in the drawing does not mean every Mustang has them.

topics.title: Steering Wheel Switch Illumination
topics.summary: This illumination sheet connects the steering wheel switch groups and paddle switches with their lighting circuits. It shows how electrical paths pass through the clockspring while the steering wheel remains free to turn.

sections.title: Keeping connections through a rotating wheel
sections.body: The clockspring contains a flexible electrical connection that accommodates steering-wheel rotation. Here, it forms part of the illumination path serving controls on the wheel. A lighting feed and return allow switch lighting to work without using rigid wires that would twist each time the driver steers.

sections.title: Why paddle switches appear on a lighting sheet
sections.body: The sheet names upshift and downshift paddle switches alongside the left and right upper and lower steering wheel switches. A control can appear in several diagrams because its lighting and its command function are different circuits. This sheet helps follow the illumination relationship among those components.

sections.title: Following the electrical references
sections.body: Connector labels identify the switch and clockspring connections, while G202 identifies a ground reference. The continuation marked for cluster and panel illumination links this sheet to the wider lighting circuit. These references describe electrical connectivity; their placement on the page does not map the wires’ physical route around the steering column.

topics.title: Wiper Switch Module Power and Network
topics.summary: This wiper-and-washer sheet shows the steering column control module’s electrical supply and network connections. The module reads the driver’s switch requests and participates in coordinating wiper operation.

sections.title: The switch request becomes control information
sections.body: The steering column control module (SCCM) monitors the multifunction switch used for wiper and washer requests. The related system description explains that those requests reach the wiper motor through a Local Interconnect Network (LIN) circuit. This page focuses on the SCCM’s supporting connections rather than the complete motor-control path.

sections.title: Why the wiper system needs network information
sections.body: The high-speed Controller Area Network (CAN) pair connects the SCCM to other vehicle modules. Information such as vehicle speed supports speed-dependent wiping, while wiper status can support wiper-activated headlamps. These communication functions are separate from the battery supply and ground that keep the SCCM electrically available.

sections.title: Reading supply and communication labels
sections.body: Battery voltage is labeled VBATT and ground is labeled GND. The fused supply comes through the body control module (BCM), with an always-live designation, while the paired network lines continue to communications sheets. The always-live label describes module power availability, not a command for the wipers to run.

topics.title: Headlamp Requests Through the Steering Column
topics.summary: This headlamp sheet shows the multifunction switch and Steering Column Control Module (SCCM) with their power, ground and communication connections. It explains the electrical foundation for sending switch information through the vehicle network.

sections.title: A switch request becomes information
sections.body: The multifunction switch supplies driver input to the steering-column electronics. A controller can communicate that input as a message, allowing another controller to operate the lighting outputs. This is why a headlamp diagram includes network wiring even though those communication wires do not carry the current that illuminates the lamps.

sections.title: Power and communication have different jobs
sections.body: The sheet identifies a fused battery supply associated with the Body Control Module (BCM), a ground connection and the paired High-Speed Controller Area Network 2 (HS2-CAN) lines. Supply and ground operate the SCCM; the paired network lines carry messages. Losing either function can interrupt the chain between driver input and lighting response.

sections.title: Following the sheet beyond its boundaries
sections.body: The module-communications references continue the network onto other sheets, while S209 and G202 identify a splice and ground point. Hot at all times describes the supply’s availability, not a command to turn on the headlamps. This schematic shows electrical relationships rather than the physical route of the steering-column harness.

topics.title: Left Headlamp Power and Control
topics.summary: This sheet shows the left headlamp's supply, relay, control and ground connections for the labeled headlamp-leveling arrangement. It identifies a high-intensity discharge (HID) system, whose light source uses a controlled electrical discharge.

sections.title: Supply and beam control have distinct roles
sections.body: The headlamp needs electrical energy to produce light, while control circuits determine its requested beam operation. The diagram separates high and low control labels from supply and ground connections. That separation helps explain why the presence of a power source alone does not establish that every headlamp function is available.

sections.title: Relay and module outputs share the job
sections.body: The battery junction box (BJB) contains the shown protected supply and left-headlamp relay. The body control module (BCM) also provides labeled field-effect transistor (FET) outputs, meaning electronic switching stages. The sheet brings those different control elements together so their relationship to the lamp can be traced.

sections.title: Read grounds and supply labels separately
sections.body: Always-powered labels describe the availability of supply at the marked points, not continuous illumination. The headlamp's ground connections lead to identified grounding references, while connector and splice labels support tracing between sheets. The headlamp-leveling qualification matters; this arrangement should not be assumed to represent every headlamp configuration.

topics.title: Right-hand discharge-headlamp power and control
topics.summary: The right-hand High-Intensity Discharge (HID) headlamp uses an electrical arc to produce its light. This sheet separates the assembly's protected supply, relay, beam-control connections and grounds.

sections.title: Lighting needs both energy and a selection
sections.body: The Battery Junction Box (BJB) provides the protected supply and right-hand headlamp relay shown here. The Body Control Module (BCM) has separate high- and low-beam outputs, identified as field-effect transistor (FET) circuits. These control connections and the main supply have different roles in producing the requested lighting state.

sections.title: The drawing separates shared and local paths
sections.body: The headlamp assembly has multiple connections, including ground paths that return through the named ground network. Showing supply, control and return together helps explain why a lighting concern may involve more than the light source itself. A missing supply and an incorrect beam command affect operation through different electrical mechanisms.

sections.title: Retain the headlamp equipment labels
sections.body: The HID and headlamp-leveling labels qualify this arrangement. Right-front beam labels identify the controlled side, and hot at all times describes supply availability rather than whether the lamp is illuminated. Connector, splice and ground identifiers link the sheet to supporting references; the schematic does not show physical harness routing.

topics.title: Rear Fog and Reverse Lamp Wiring
topics.summary: This sheet shows the rear fog lamp wiring and its relationship to the reverse-lamp circuit. It connects the lamp functions to the Body Control Module (BCM), intermediate connections and the ground return.

sections.title: Two lighting jobs at the rear
sections.body: A rear fog lamp makes the vehicle more visible from behind in poor visibility, while a reverse lamp indicates reversing and illuminates the area behind the car. The drawing labels these functions separately, even where their wiring passes through the same connector or lamp assembly.

sections.title: Electronic outputs control the lamps
sections.body: The BCM outputs are marked as Field-Effect Transistor (FET) circuits, meaning electronic switching controls the lamp feeds. The ground path completes the electrical circuit. A supply marked 'Hot at all times' remains available independently of ignition position; that label alone does not mean the lamp stays illuminated.

sections.title: Following connections across the sheet
sections.body: Circuit identifiers and wire colors distinguish the rear fog feed, reverse feed and ground as they pass through connectors and splices. The references lead to supporting connector and ground information. This is a map of electrical relationships; the line positions do not describe the harness route through the body.

topics.title: Door-handle ambient lighting circuits
topics.summary: The front door-handle ambient lamps provide colored interior accent lighting. This sheet connects both lamps to body control module B through separate color channels and a shared return circuit.

sections.title: Combining color channels
sections.body: Red, green, and blue lighting channels can combine to produce different visible colors. Changing their relative output changes the mixture seen at the lamp. The diagram labels those channels separately from RETURN, making the electrical roles clearer than a single generic lamp symbol would.

sections.title: Comparing both door lamps
sections.body: The left-hand (LH) and right-hand (RH) door-handle lamps connect into the same labeled ambient-lighting network. This lets the reader distinguish a path shared by both lamps from an individual lamp connection. A common connection concern could affect both sides without requiring two independent lamp failures.

sections.title: Following channels across the sheet
sections.body: Circuit labels CLN44, CLN45, and CLN46 identify the color-channel paths, while RLN44 identifies the return. Connector and splice references show where those paths continue or join. The lettered continuations lead to other interior-lighting sheets; their placement on the page does not represent physical harness routing.

topics.title: Illuminated Scuff Plate Wiring
topics.summary: Illuminated scuff plates add ambient lighting at the door sills when the vehicle has this equipment. This sheet connects the driver and passenger lamps to their color-control circuits.

sections.title: Separate color channels create the illumination
sections.body: Body Control Module B has outputs labeled red, green, and blue for this lighting branch. Controlling the contribution of these color channels allows a lamp to produce different colors. The lamp connections also include a shared return path, which completes the relevant circuits rather than selecting a color.

sections.title: Why both door sills appear together
sections.body: The driver and passenger scuff-plate lamps connect to common color circuits through splices. Showing both branches makes that shared relationship clear. A concern affecting the same color at both lamps could involve a common path, while a concern at one lamp requires attention to how its individual branch differs.

sections.title: Matching channel names to circuit identifiers
sections.body: The equipment note restricts this drawing to lighted scuff plates. Circuit identifiers and splice labels provide continuity through changes in wire color, while continuation references connect to other interior-lighting sheets. The red, green, and blue output labels describe lighting channels; they should not be assumed to match every conductor’s insulation color.

topics.title: Rear Stop, Turn, and Parking Lamp Wiring
topics.summary: This sheet shows the rear lamp connections for vehicles outside the China and Europe applications. It separates parking-light power from the inner, middle, and outer stop-and-turn channels.

sections.title: Each lamp assembly contains several functions
sections.body: The rear assemblies provide parking illumination and separately connected stop-and-turn sections. Body Control Module B has individual connections for the inner, middle, and outer sections, plus an outage-related connection. This separation lets the electrical reference distinguish one segment’s circuit from the common housing that contains all of them.

sections.title: Why two body-control modules appear
sections.body: The body control module (BCM) supplies the position-lamp paths shown with field-effect transistor (FET) outputs, while Body Control Module B connects to the segmented stop-and-turn functions. Both rear assemblies also use the shared ground reference. A functioning parking lamp therefore does not establish that every stop-and-turn circuit is intact.

sections.title: Tracing a function before comparing sides
sections.body: Follow the named lamp function, circuit identifier, and connector reference together when comparing left and right assemblies. The outage label identifies an additional circuit rather than another illuminated segment. The market exclusions are essential, and the schematic establishes electrical connections without specifying a physical harness route or the timing of lamp operation.

topics.title: Rear Lamp Control Circuits
topics.summary: This sheet separates the parking, turn, stop and outage-related connections at the rear lamp assemblies. Its China and Europe label limits the application of the circuit arrangement shown.

sections.title: One assembly performs several lighting jobs
sections.body: A rear lamp assembly can contain several electrical functions within one housing. Parking illumination marks the vehicle's presence, stop lighting communicates braking, and turn lighting signals direction. Separate labeled connections let the diagram distinguish these functions even though they share the same physical lamp assembly.

sections.title: Control outputs and outage circuits differ
sections.body: The body control module (BCM) shows field-effect transistor (FET) output stages, which are electronic switches controlling lamp circuits. Body control module B also appears on outage-labeled connections. Those outage paths concern lamp-status information and should be distinguished from the feeds that produce the visible lighting functions.

sections.title: Trace each side with its own labels
sections.body: Left-hand and right-hand assemblies have separately identified connectors, alongside a shared ground reference and continuation markers. Follow the park, turn, stop and outage labels rather than assuming adjacent lines perform the same task. The sheet maps electrical relationships for its stated markets, not the physical layout inside either lamp.

topics.title: Mirror turn-signal circuit connections
topics.summary: The exterior-mirror turn lamps repeat the vehicle’s direction indication where other road users can see it. This without-memory wiring sheet connects their branches to body-control outputs and grounds, with China-specific continuations to the rear-lamp circuits.

sections.title: Electronic outputs control the indication
sections.body: The Body Control Module (BCM) has outputs labeled for the left and right rear turn lamps, with field-effect transistor (FET) switching identified on the drawing. The sheet traces related turn-signal branches to the exterior mirrors. These electronic outputs switch lamp circuits in response to the vehicle's signaling commands.

sections.title: The mirror branch belongs to a larger circuit
sections.body: The continuation references connect this page to the wider turn-signal, stoplamp and hazard-lamp diagram. Splices show where conductors join, and the mirror grounds complete their electrical paths. This context helps distinguish a concern limited to a mirror branch from one involving a connection shared with other lamps.

sections.title: Observe the market and equipment labels
sections.body: WITHOUT MEMORY is the heading for the whole sheet. The smaller dashed China outlines qualify the branches continuing to sheet 90-6; they do not make the entire mirror circuit China-only. Hot at all times describes supply availability, not continuous illumination. Left-hand and right-hand mirror identifiers separate the sides, while connector and ground references lead to their supporting views.

topics.title: Front Parking and Turn Lamp Circuits
topics.summary: This sheet shows the Body Control Module (BCM) connections for the front side turn-signal lamps and their parking-light functions. Separate controlled outputs allow each lamp assembly to provide steady position lighting and flashing turn indications.

sections.title: Different functions share each assembly
sections.body: The lamp symbols contain separate TURN and PARK labels. Parking illumination makes the vehicle visible, while the turn function provides a changing directional signal. Separate circuits let the controller operate these functions independently even though they share a lamp assembly and a ground connection.

sections.title: Electronic outputs replace simple direct switching
sections.body: The BCM outputs are marked as field-effect transistor (FET) outputs, meaning electronic switches control the lamp circuits. The sheet separates left and right front turn outputs from left and right position-lamp outputs. This arrangement helps explain why one lighting function can be affected while another at the same assembly still works.

sections.title: Tracing feed and shared return
sections.body: Connector identifiers C1042 and C156 distinguish the right and left assemblies. The ground circuit runs through the referenced splice and ground point, S121 and G102. The hot-at-all-times notation identifies supply availability in the diagram; it does not mean the controlled lamps remain illuminated continuously.

topics.title: Rear marker and license-plate lamps
topics.summary: Rear side-marker lamps make the vehicle’s rear sides visible, while license-plate lamps illuminate the plate. This sheet shows their shared parking-lamp supply and ground branches.

sections.title: A controlled feed serving several lamps
sections.body: The body control module (BCM) provides the parking-lamp output shown here through a field-effect transistor (FET), an electronic switching device. The lamps connect as separate branches of the labeled supply and return paths. Each needs both paths intact for current to flow through its light source.

sections.title: Why shared branches are useful
sections.body: The left and right rear side markers and both license-plate lamps appear together because they share circuit relationships. A fault before a branch point can affect several lamps, while a fault confined to one branch may affect only that lamp. The drawing helps distinguish those possibilities.

sections.title: Tracing supply, splices, and ground
sections.body: CLS30 identifies the supply path, GD301 the ground path, and G400 the ground connection. S418 and S419 identify splices, with connector references linking the harness sections. The 'Hot at all times' notation describes supply availability in the diagram; it does not mean the lamps remain continuously illuminated.

topics.title: Passenger Power Window Wiring
topics.summary: This sheet shows passenger-door window control on vehicles without memory equipment. It connects the local switch and regulator motor with power, ground, door-status, and global-window circuits.

sections.title: Switch requests control glass movement
sections.body: The regulator motor provides the mechanical drive that raises and lowers the door glass. Its connections include up and down requests as well as battery power, delayed-accessory power, ground, and other control inputs. This arrangement separates the request to move from the electrical energy needed to drive the window.

sections.title: Why door and global inputs appear here
sections.body: The motor assembly has connections labeled ajar and global in addition to the local switch paths. They show that window operation depends on more than the passenger pressing a button. Body Control Module B and the remote-entry continuation link this window circuit to wider vehicle commands and door-related information.

sections.title: Following power feeds and equipment notes
sections.body: The body control module (BCM) supplies fused circuits and contains the non-serviceable accessory-delay relay. Ground and splice references reveal shared portions of the wiring. The without-memory designation and convertible continuation must be respected, while automatic-up and automatic-down switch labels identify requests rather than separate window motors.

topics.title: Memory-switch inputs at the driver door
topics.summary: The Driver Door Module (DDM) receives door-mounted inputs and communicates with other vehicle electronics. This power-window sheet shows its supply, ground, network connection and memory-setting switch circuits on the memory-equipped configuration.

sections.title: A switch input becomes module information
sections.body: The memory-set switch provides separate selection paths and a return to the DDM. Pressing a selection changes the corresponding input so the module can recognize the request. These input wires carry command information; the seat motors themselves are not shown as loads on this portion of the diagram.

sections.title: Door electronics link several features
sections.body: The sheet places memory controls within the wider power-window wiring because they connect through the same door module. A protected feed from the Battery Junction Box (BJB) powers the module, and a ground completes the circuit. The medium-speed Controller Area Network (CAN) provides its communication connection to the rest of the vehicle.

sections.title: Separate supply, selection and network paths
sections.body: VBATT identifies battery supply, GND identifies ground, and the paired network labels identify communication wiring. The SET labels identify individual memory-switch inputs. Hot at all times describes when the supply is available, while the continuation and network references lead beyond this sheet; they do not depict the harness's physical route.

topics.title: Passenger-window control on memory-equipped vehicles
topics.summary: The passenger-window regulator motor raises and lowers the door glass. This sheet shows how power, door-module commands and shared window inputs reach it on vehicles with memory equipment.

sections.title: Motor power and direction commands are separate
sections.body: The motor assembly has battery supply, ground and delayed-accessory connections, together with up and down inputs from the Passenger Door Module (PDM). Power provides the energy to move the glass; direction inputs request the movement. Keeping those roles distinct makes the circuit easier to understand than treating every wire as a motor feed.

sections.title: The window also receives shared information
sections.body: A global input connects the motor to Body Control Module B, and an ajar input provides door-state information. These paths explain why the local window is part of wider vehicle operation. The Body Control Module (BCM) also contains the delayed-accessory relay shown here, linking window electrical availability to accessory-power control.

sections.title: Keep the equipment qualification in view
sections.body: MEMORY is the sheet’s equipment qualification. The convertible note applies specifically to the continuation through C314 toward the rear-window sheet, rather than restricting the entire passenger-door circuit to convertibles. The accessory-delay relay is identified as non-serviceable, so its symbol does not imply a removable plug-in part. Supply labels, ground references and continuation markers connect this sheet to the supporting diagrams.

topics.title: Passenger Door Module Shared Circuits
topics.summary: This power-window sheet shows Passenger Door Module (PDM) connections for memory mirrors and door-lock functions. It explains how a module associated with the window system also participates in other passenger-door equipment.

sections.title: Mirror movement needs feedback
sections.body: The mirror motor paths control horizontal and vertical movement, while potentiometer paths report mirror position. A potentiometer changes its electrical output with movement, allowing a memory system to relate a commanded position to the mirror's actual position. The sheet also names mirror heating and turn-indicator connections.

sections.title: Why lock circuits share the sheet
sections.body: Lock, unlock, return and status labels appear alongside the mirror circuits because the PDM connects several door functions. Their references continue into remote keyless entry and alarm information. Understanding that shared connection point helps explain why the power-window section contains circuits that perform other jobs.

sections.title: Trace the named function onward
sections.body: Connector identifiers separate the PDM connections, and circuit names distinguish motor outputs, position feedback and lock-related signals. The memory qualifier limits the arrangement shown. Cross-references lead to the relevant power-mirror or entry-system sheet; this excerpt does not itself show a complete window-motor circuit or physical harness route.

topics.title: Overhead Console Electrical Functions
topics.summary: The overhead console brings together map lamps, microphone connections and intrusion-related circuitry shown on this sheet. Its wiring combines operating power, lighting control, communication and audio paths that serve different purposes within the same assembly.

sections.title: Several functions share the console
sections.body: The driver and passenger map lamps turn electrical energy into cabin light, while the microphone converts sound into an electrical signal for the audio system. The intrusion-sense label identifies another function in the assembly. Sharing a housing does not make these functions electrically interchangeable or give them a common command path.

sections.title: How the body controller fits in
sections.body: The Body Control Module (BCM) appears with interior-lighting control, a battery-saver relay and a Local Interconnect Network (LIN) connection. The lighting output is marked as a field-effect transistor (FET) circuit. These labels distinguish switched lighting power from communication, while the battery-saver function provides a means of limiting lamp-related battery use.

sections.title: Tracing audio separately from lighting
sections.body: The microphone’s positive, negative and shield paths continue toward the audio/navigation references. The shield helps protect a sensitive audio signal from electrical interference. Ground, splice and connector labels locate the other circuit relationships. The relay’s non-serviceable label describes its service arrangement; its symbol should not be read as a separate replaceable relay.

topics.title: Door Handle Lighting and Lock Indicators
topics.summary: This sheet covers interior front-door handle lighting and door-lock indicators on vehicles without memory equipment. It shows their connections to the body-control electronics and continuing entry-and-alarm circuits.

sections.title: Illumination and lock indication serve different purposes
sections.body: The handle ambient lamp makes the interior handle easier to see, while the door-lock indicator communicates lock status. Although both appear within the same door-related assembly, their circuit functions should remain distinct. A lighting concern therefore needs to be related to the correct function rather than assumed to involve the door latch.

sections.title: Control and return paths cross the door connections
sections.body: The drawing includes the body control module (BCM), Body Control Module B, a return connection, and a delayed-accessory output marked as a field-effect transistor (FET). Harness junctions carry these circuits toward both front doors. A return path completes the relevant circuit, while a controlled output determines when electrical energy is available.

sections.title: Following the without-memory version
sections.body: The equipment note limits this sheet to vehicles without memory. Left-hand and right-hand lamp labels identify the two door branches, and continuation references connect them to other remote keyless entry and alarm sheets. Repeated wire colors alone are insufficient for tracing; the circuit identifiers distinguish their electrical roles.

topics.title: Door Lock Indicator and Handle Lighting
topics.summary: This remote-entry sheet shows electrical connections for door-lock indicators and interior door-handle ambient lamps. The diagram is marked for the memory-equipped arrangement and includes both door modules and body control module B.

sections.title: Light reports status rather than moving the lock
sections.body: A door-lock indicator provides visible information about locking status, while ambient handle lighting makes the handle area visible. These lighting functions differ from the actuator that physically moves a lock. The sheet's status and return labels help separate indication circuits from the mechanical locking function.

sections.title: Both doors share part of the circuit structure
sections.body: The driver door module (DDM) and passenger door module (PDM) each have a status-labeled connection. Body control module B provides the named return relationship, with a splice connecting branches. Showing both doors together makes the shared path visible while preserving the separate status connection for each side.

sections.title: Follow status, return and continuation labels
sections.body: Left-hand and right-hand lamp connectors are identified separately, and continuation marks link this page with the rest of the entry-and-alarm circuitry. Follow those labels rather than interpreting every brown wire as the same function. The memory qualification limits applicability and does not establish the layout of vehicles without that equipment.

topics.title: Keyless Entry Radio Module Circuits
topics.summary: This sheet shows the Radio Transceiver Module (RTM) within the remote keyless-entry and alarm system. It connects the radio interface to operating power, ground and communication paths used by the vehicle’s electronic controls.

sections.title: Radio communication meets vehicle wiring
sections.body: A transceiver handles radio communication, allowing information from a remote device to enter the vehicle’s electronic system without a physical wire to the key. The RTM’s wired connections then link that radio function with the rest of the car. Its presence does not mean it directly powers every lock or alarm device.

sections.title: Power and two communication paths
sections.body: The sheet identifies a fused battery supply, ground and Medium-Speed Controller Area Network (MS-CAN) pair. It also shows a separate K-line connection to the Body Control Module (BCM). These paths have different purposes: power operates the module, while the communication connections carry information between electronic components.

sections.title: Understanding supply availability and continuations
sections.body: Hot at all times describes the availability of the battery supply, which supports functions needed while the vehicle is parked. It does not mean every associated output is continuously active. Network continuation references lead to the wider communication diagrams, while connector and ground identifiers tie this sheet to the corresponding physical reference views.

topics.title: Alarm Intrusion Sensing and Security Horn Wiring
topics.summary: This sheet connects overhead-console intrusion sensing with the body control module and the security horn relay. It shows the electrical support and communication paths used by these alarm components.

sections.title: Detection and warning have separate roles
sections.body: Intrusion sensing provides information about activity inside the vehicle, while the security horn provides an audible alarm output. The body control module (BCM) is part of the control relationship shown here. A detection concern and a horn concern can therefore involve different branches of the same alarm system.

sections.title: Recognizing supply, ground, and communication
sections.body: Battery voltage, marked VBATT, supplies electrical energy; ground, marked GND, completes the supply circuit. The Local Interconnect Network (LIN) connection carries communication rather than horn operating current. The always-live supply labels explain how alarm-related circuits can remain powered with the ignition off, without implying that every component is continuously active.

sections.title: Using the sheet as an electrical map
sections.body: Connector identifiers, wire colors, circuit labels, and the shared ground reference let you follow connections into other sheets. The security horn relay is identified as non-serviceable. Unused connections should remain distinct from active circuits, and the schematic’s arrangement describes electrical relationships rather than the physical route of the harness.

topics.title: Driver Seat Heating and Cooling Circuits
topics.summary: This sheet connects the left front seat’s cushion and backrest blower assemblies with the front seat climate-control module. It separates airflow control, temperature information and thermoelectric-device circuits within the climate-controlled seat system.

sections.title: Air movement and heat transfer work together
sections.body: The cushion and backrest each have a blower assembly that moves air through the seat. Thermoelectric devices transfer heat electrically, while temperature information lets the controller monitor conditions. These different jobs explain why each assembly has more wiring than a basic motor that only turns on and off.

sections.title: Why the diagram separates circuit families
sections.body: The labels distinguish blower control, sensor paths and thermoelectric device (TED) connections. Seat Control Module E (SCME), described here as the front seat climate-control module, links those functions. Separating the paths helps explain how airflow, temperature feedback and thermal output can be affected differently by a circuit concern.

sections.title: Following cushion and backrest connections
sections.body: The named cushion and backrest assemblies provide the clearest starting points for reading the sheet. Connector identifiers and the referenced splices carry their circuits through the harness to the module. Repeated wire labels identify continuing electrical paths; the drawing’s arrangement does not show the wires’ physical route inside the seat.

topics.title: Right Front Climate-Controlled Seat Wiring
topics.summary: This sheet connects the right-hand front seat’s cushion and backrest climate-control assemblies to their controller. It separates airflow control, thermoelectric operation, and temperature feedback.

sections.title: Airflow carries the heating or cooling effect
sections.body: The cushion and backrest each have a blower assembly. Air movement distributes the temperature effect through the seat, while a thermoelectric device (TED) changes temperature using electrical energy. Temperature-sensor connections provide feedback, allowing the controller to relate its commands to the conditions developing within each assembly.

sections.title: Why each assembly needs several circuits
sections.body: The front seat climate control module has separate connections for blower control, thermoelectric drive, and sensor information. These are different electrical jobs: moving air requires motor power, changing temperature requires device power, and measuring temperature requires a signal and reference path. Combining them in one assembly does not make their circuits interchangeable.

sections.title: Following cushion and backrest labels
sections.body: The repeated cushion and backrest label patterns help distinguish the two branches. Positive and negative drive labels belong to their respective loads, while sensor-return labels identify measurement paths. Connector and splice references show electrical continuity through the harness; the drawing does not describe the physical airflow passages inside the seat.

topics.title: Power mirrors without heat or memory
topics.summary: Power-mirror motors change the angle of the reflective glass so the driver can adjust the rearward view. This diagram applies to mirrors without heating or memory and shows their switch, motor, supply, and ground relationships.

sections.title: Reversing a motor changes direction
sections.body: Each mirror has motor functions for horizontal and vertical movement. The switch arrangement reverses electrical polarity to reverse a motor’s direction, allowing adjustment both ways along each axis. The direction labels in the drawing describe these movements rather than separate motors for every individual direction.

sections.title: How the driver’s control reaches both mirrors
sections.body: The exterior-mirror control is shown with the master window control switch assembly. Its circuits select the driver or passenger mirror and the desired movement. The supply comes through the body control module (BCM) accessory-delay arrangement, while the ground network completes the switch’s electrical connection.

sections.title: Following the applicable mirror circuit
sections.body: Motor symbols and polarity markings explain movement, while connector and splice references show the electrical path to each side. The G301 reference identifies the ground connection. The explicit 'without heated mirrors' and 'without memory' qualifiers are essential; this sheet does not describe heater operation or memory-position electronics.

topics.title: SYNC and Positioning Module Wiring
topics.summary: This audio-navigation sheet shows power, ground and network connections for the SYNC module and Global Positioning System Module (GPSM). It explains how these units receive electrical supply and exchange information with the vehicle.

sections.title: Multimedia and position information
sections.body: The GPSM supplies positioning information, while the SYNC module, also identified as the Accessory Protocol Interface Module (APIM), supports the multimedia interface. The sheet focuses on the connections that let these units operate and communicate. It does not show speaker outputs or the complete navigation signal chain.

sections.title: Supply paths differ from message paths
sections.body: Battery-voltage and ground labels describe the operating supply, with the Body Control Module (BCM) and fuse reference shown upstream. The 'Hot at all times' notation describes supply availability. Medium-speed and high-speed Controller Area Network (CAN) pairs carry messages separately from the wires supplying electrical energy.

sections.title: Follow the named network branch
sections.body: The distinct CAN labels identify different communication branches, while connector, splice and ground references help trace their relationships. The coupe notation is an applicability cue attached to the illustrated wiring and should remain with that detail. Continuation references extend the electrical diagram; they do not indicate physical harness routing.

topics.title: Audio Power, Antennas and Network Links
topics.summary: This audio-system sheet connects the audio control module (ACM) with its power, ground, antenna and communication paths. It helps explain how broadcast signals reach the radio while vehicle electrical information reaches the same unit through other circuits.

sections.title: Radio signals and vehicle messages differ
sections.body: Coaxial cables carry weak antenna signals within a shield that limits unwanted interference. Separate wires provide electrical power and ground. The high-speed controller area network (HS-CAN) connection carries vehicle messages, while the amplitude-modulation and frequency-modulation (AM/FM) antenna paths carry the broadcasts the radio receives.

sections.title: Several supporting systems appear together
sections.body: The sheet includes the battery junction box, antenna amplifier, body and powertrain control modules, and a starter-related branch. It also identifies a global positioning system (GPS) and satellite digital audio radio service (SDARS) antenna. These connections explain why radio reception, electrical supply and vehicle-state information require different tracing paths.

sections.title: Follow body-style and branch labels
sections.body: The coupe's on-glass antenna and the convertible arrangement are explicitly distinguished. Engine labels near the starting circuitry qualify those branches rather than the whole audio system. Ground, shield, switched-supply and always-powered labels describe electrical function; connector references and continuation markers lead to supporting sheets, not physical cable routes.

topics.title: Audio processing module power and data
topics.summary: The audio digital signal processing (DSP) module shapes audio signals within the sound system. This diagram shows the electrical supply, ground, and network connections that support its operation.

sections.title: Processing sound needs power and information
sections.body: Digital audio processing can alter characteristics such as frequency balance before sound reaches the speakers. The module needs electrical power to perform that work and communication paths to exchange operating information. The paired network wires shown here carry data; they are separate from the module’s battery supply and ground.

sections.title: Why this sheet separates support circuits
sections.body: The drawing identifies a fused feed associated with the body control module (BCM), a G201 ground connection, and high-speed controller area network 3 (HS3 CAN) connections. Separating these roles helps explain how a module can have a supply concern, a return-path concern, or a communication concern.

sections.title: Reading battery and network labels
sections.body: VBATT denotes battery voltage, GND denotes ground, and the CAN plus and minus labels identify the paired communication circuits. 'Hot at all times' describes the feed’s availability, rather than continuous audio playback. Connector and page references continue the electrical trace without specifying the module’s physical harness route.

topics.title: Rear Subwoofer and Amplifier Wiring
topics.summary: The rear subwoofer produces low-frequency sound using power from its own amplifier. This sheet separates the audio signal, amplifier enable command, electrical supply, and speaker output.

sections.title: A small audio signal controls larger speaker current
sections.body: The digital signal processing (DSP) module sends the subwoofer audio signal to the rear amplifier. The amplifier uses its battery supply to produce the current needed to move the subwoofer cone. Its enable connection has a separate role: it controls amplifier operation rather than carrying the bass audio itself.

sections.title: Why power and shielding are shown separately
sections.body: The diagram includes a fused supply from the body control module (BCM), a ground connection, and shielding associated with the audio wiring. Shielding reduces unwanted electrical interference in the signal path. An always-live supply can be available while the amplifier remains inactive because supply availability and the enable command are separate conditions.

sections.title: Following the signal through the amplifier
sections.body: Read the positive and negative subwoofer labels in relation to the component boundary: the amplifier has an incoming audio pair and an outgoing speaker pair. Those labels do not make every negative audio conductor a chassis ground. Connector and ground references help distinguish signal continuity from the amplifier’s power circuit.

topics.title: Steering-wheel audio and menu inputs
topics.summary: The upper steering-wheel switches provide menu-selection and audio-control inputs without requiring the driver to reach the center controls. This sheet shows their electrical paths through the clockspring to the steering-column controller.

sections.title: Button presses become electrical inputs
sections.body: The left upper group contains directional and confirmation controls, while the right upper group includes volume and other selection buttons. Their circuits lead to the Steering Column Control Module (SCCM). The module interprets switch inputs so the requested action can be handled by the relevant vehicle electronics.

sections.title: The wheel must remain connected while turning
sections.body: The clockspring provides a flexible electrical connection between the rotating steering wheel and fixed column. This sheet includes that transition because the switch path passes through it. It also references cluster and panel illumination, showing that button lighting and button-command circuits are related parts of the wheel assembly with different jobs.

sections.title: Keep input and illumination paths distinct
sections.body: Analog-to-digital (A/D) labels identify an input channel and associated returns used by the column electronics. The ground reference and illumination references lead to supporting circuit information. Trace each named switch group separately: sharing a clockspring or ground area does not make the left and right buttons the same electrical input.

topics.title: Passenger seat-switch contact testing
topics.summary: The right-hand (RH) front seat control switch selects horizontal, height, and tilt movement on the six-way seat. This reference describes which internal contacts should connect when each direction is selected.

sections.title: Selecting movement through contacts
sections.body: Moving the switch changes which electrical paths are joined inside it. The paired contact arrangements support opposite directions of seat movement, such as forward and rearward. Those internal connections are the switch’s contribution to the system; the motors and seat mechanism provide the actual movement.

sections.title: Why continuity is checked separately
sections.body: A closed circuit means the selected contacts provide an electrical path between the specified points. The chart tests that switching behavior independently of whether the seat moves. This distinction matters because a seat-motion concern can involve the switch, its external wiring, a motor, or the mechanical mechanism.

sections.title: Matching direction, circuit, and connector view
sections.body: The table groups horizontal, height, and tilt functions and gives the expected result for each switch position. The schematic explains contact relationships, while the connector view identifies their physical arrangement at C3190. Both are needed to interpret the chart; the connector drawing alone does not show switching behavior.

topics.title: Passenger Window Switch Contact Test
topics.summary: The passenger window switch changes electrical connections to request upward or downward glass movement. This component-testing sheet describes the contact patterns associated with its rest, directional and one-touch positions.

sections.title: Switch movement changes circuit continuity
sections.body: Inside the switch, moving contacts join or separate particular electrical paths. The window-control circuitry interprets those changes as requests. The one-touch positions provide a distinguishable switching pattern, allowing the control system to recognize a different request from an ordinary held upward or downward input.

sections.title: A contact test isolates one component's behavior
sections.body: This reference focuses on whether the switch makes the expected connections in each position. It does not directly evaluate the regulator mechanism or motor's ability to move the glass. Separating contact behavior from window movement helps distinguish a switch-level observation from the performance of the complete system.

sections.title: Open and closed describe electrical paths
sections.body: A closed circuit means the listed path is connected; an open circuit means it is interrupted. The no-voltage heading identifies a passive contact test rather than powered system operation. The schematic and male connector view establish how the chart relates to the switch, with the technical table supplying the exact combinations.

topics.title: Understanding a Power Relay Test
topics.summary: A power relay uses an electromagnet to switch a separate electrical load circuit. This reference compares its coil, contacts, and electrical isolation in resting and energized states.

sections.title: A magnetic coil moves the contact
sections.body: Current through the relay coil produces a magnetic field that moves its internal contact. The contact then joins the load-side conductors shown in the schematic. This allows a control circuit to operate a separate power circuit without requiring the control switch to carry the load’s full current.

sections.title: Why the reference checks more than continuity
sections.body: The unpowered checks address coil resistance, the resting contact state, and isolation between coil and contact circuits. Each describes a different part of relay health. A coil can have electrical continuity while a damaged contact still fails to pass power, so one satisfactory reading does not establish complete relay operation.

sections.title: Reading resting and energized results
sections.body: The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) relay drawing relates the male connector view to the internal schematic. An open circuit is the expected result for some unpowered checks, rather than automatically a failure. The separate energized test evaluates switching behavior; its setup and limits belong to the technical procedure.

topics.title: Understanding the headlamp-switch test chart
topics.summary: The headlamp switch provides electrical selections for exterior lighting and related controls. This component-test sheet describes the expected open or closed contact states as the switch is moved between its listed positions.

sections.title: Switch positions change electrical continuity
sections.body: Inside a switch, moving the control changes which contacts connect. A closed circuit provides an electrical path between the specified contacts, while an open circuit separates them. These changes encode selections such as parking lamps, headlamps or automatic lighting so the associated vehicle circuitry can respond.

sections.title: The chart checks a pattern of behavior
sections.body: A switch must create the appropriate contact pattern across its operating positions, not merely produce continuity somewhere. The chart pairs each tested circuit with the relevant position and expected result. This makes the reference useful for understanding contact behavior separately from the condition of downstream lamps, wiring or control modules.

sections.title: Keep each result aligned with its row
sections.body: The connector drawing establishes the face orientation, and the table links the selected contacts to functions such as dimming and fog lighting. Read the circuit, control position and expected state together. Equipment-dependent labels describe the shown switch configuration; their presence does not mean every Mustang has every listed lighting function.

topics.title: Finding front-end electrical components
topics.summary: This location view identifies electrical components, connectors, grounds, and splices around the vehicle’s front area. It connects a name or identifier from a circuit diagram to the component’s illustrated position on the car.

sections.title: Several systems in one area
sections.body: The view includes exterior lamps and their controllers, the horn, wheel-speed sensors, front impact sensors, and engine air-measurement sensors. It also labels the active grille shutter, proximity radar, washer pump, hood switch, and air-conditioning components. Nearby parts can serve very different sensing, warning, or operating functions.

sections.title: Why exact identification matters
sections.body: Ambient-air, intake-air, and turbocharger boost-pressure sensors measure different conditions even though all relate to air. Likewise, a wheel-speed sensor and an impact sensor provide different vehicle information. Finding the named component prevents a nearby connector from being mistaken for the one discussed in a diagnostic procedure.

sections.title: Using the grid and identifiers
sections.body: The letter-and-number grid provides a visual reference, while C, G, and S identifiers distinguish connectors, grounds, and splices. Left-hand (LH) and right-hand (RH) labels separate paired components. The view covers equipment-dependent items, so each label must be matched to the vehicle rather than assumed present.

topics.title: Finding 2.3L Engine Components
topics.summary: This location sheet identifies engine sensors, fuel components, and related connections on the 2.3L application. It connects component names used in electrical references with their positions on the vehicle.

sections.title: Different sensors report different conditions
sections.body: The coolant-temperature sensor reports engine thermal conditions, camshaft-position sensors report shaft timing, and knock sensors detect engine vibration associated with combustion. Oxygen sensors provide exhaust information. The positive crankcase ventilation valve manages crankcase vapors, while the injectors and injection pump belong to fuel delivery rather than temperature or timing measurement.

sections.title: Why precise identification matters
sections.body: The sheet distinguishes fuel pressure from fuel rail pressure, and an engine oil pressure sensor from an oil pressure switch. Similar names can represent different jobs and connections. Matching the full label prevents a diagnostic reference for one component from being applied to another simply because both mention pressure.

sections.title: Using orientation before connector numbers
sections.body: The front-of-vehicle arrow and grid establish orientation, while connector identifiers tie each callout to electrical information. Injector and sensor suffixes distinguish individual components. The transmission callout names the 6R80 assembly; the location view should be matched to the actual engine and transmission equipment rather than treated as universal.

topics.title: 3.7L Engine Component Locations
topics.summary: This location view identifies several 3.7L engine components and their electrical connection references. It helps translate a component name in a circuit or procedure into the correct physical item on the vehicle.

sections.title: Fuel, spark and position have separate roles
sections.body: Fuel injectors meter fuel, while coil-on-plug ignition units generate the spark energy for their cylinders. Crankshaft and camshaft position sensors report rotational timing. Variable camshaft timing solenoids control oil used to adjust valve events, so a position sensor and a timing solenoid are related but different components.

sections.title: Similar-looking components need precise identities
sections.body: The view distinguishes individual injectors and ignition coils, bank-specific camshaft components and several oxygen sensors. It also names the knock sensor, evaporative-emission purge valve and 6R80 transmission connection. These identifiers matter because selecting a nearby but different component can disconnect the physical observation from the circuit being investigated.

sections.title: Orient the picture before using its labels
sections.body: The front-of-vehicle arrow establishes orientation, and the grid supports locating the labeled items within the drawing. The engine label limits this view to the 3.7L application. Connector identifiers lead to connection details, while splice identifiers mark harness junction references; neither substitutes for the component's full electrical schematic.

topics.title: Transmission and Exhaust Connector Locations
topics.summary: This location view identifies reversing-switch, transmission-speed, starter and exhaust-sensor connections. It helps distinguish nearby components and the engine-specific connectors that can otherwise look similar when viewed beneath the vehicle.

sections.title: Different components report different conditions
sections.body: The reversing lamp switch indicates reverse selection, while the Output Shaft Speed (OSS) sensor reports transmission output rotation. The starter motor turns the engine for starting. Heated Oxygen Sensors (HO2S) measure oxygen remaining in exhaust gas, providing information used in engine and emissions monitoring.

sections.title: Why the engine labels matter
sections.body: The exhaust-sensor labels distinguish the 2.3L, 3.7L and 5.0L installations, with different connector identifiers for their illustrated sensors. These are alternative application references, not a statement that every listed sensor appears on every car. Matching the engine and component designation prevents a nearby sensor from being mistaken for the intended one.

sections.title: Using direction and connector identity
sections.body: The front-of-vehicle marker and reference grid orient the drawing, while the harness identifier groups the illustrated wiring. Separate starter connector labels identify connections to the same named component. This view answers where the referenced items are shown; circuit behavior and electrical relationships belong to their corresponding schematics.

topics.title: Cabin Sensor and Harness Locations
topics.summary: This location view identifies the in-vehicle temperature sensor connection and several harness splice locations. It helps translate electrical identifiers into places on the vehicle so the correct component or harness feature can be recognized.

sections.title: The temperature sensor’s purpose
sections.body: The in-vehicle temperature sensor measures cabin air temperature for the climate-control system. That information lets a controller compare actual conditions with the requested temperature. Its connection is identified as C233, distinguishing it from other temperature sensors that measure outside air or conditions elsewhere in the heating and cooling system.

sections.title: Why the splice labels are included
sections.body: The many S-prefixed identifiers mark splice locations within the illustrated harnesses. A splice joins conductors as part of a circuit, so locating one can matter when tracing a shared electrical path. Nearby splice labels do not mean all those circuits are connected together or serve the temperature sensor.

sections.title: Using the view’s orientation
sections.body: The front-of-vehicle marker establishes direction, and the lettered and numbered grid provides position references. Harness identifiers 14401 and 14B242 distinguish the assemblies shown. This is a physical-location aid: the matching wiring schematic explains what the circuits do and which of the pictured splices belong to the circuit being studied.

topics.title: Finding rear electrical components on a convertible
